stem: A question paper has two sections. Section A has 5 questions and Section B has 6 questions. A student must answer 4 questions from Section A and 3 questions from Section B. In how many ways can the student make this selection?

per_option_rationale.rationale: P(5,4) * P(6,3) = 120 * 120 ... actually P(5,4)*C(6,3) = 120*20 = 2400, treating Section A selections as ordered.

Computing only C(5,4)*C(6,2) = 5*15 = 75, or computing C(5,3)*C(6,2) = 10*15 = 150, or swapping the required counts: C(5,3)*C(6,4) = 10*15 = 150... a student who swaps the required counts and then makes an arithmetic slip gives 50 = C(5,4)*C(6,2)/3... more directly: computing only C(6,3)*C(5,1)/2 type of wrong decomposition = 50.
C(5,4)*C(6,3) + C(5,3)*C(6,4) = 100+100 = 200, treating the problem as 'at least 4 from A and at least 3 from B' and adding two cases instead of using a single fixed requirement.

explanation: The number of required questions is fixed for each section, so the selections are independent. Multiply: C(5,4) * C(6,3) = 5 * 20 = 100.

explanation_sections.punchline: Fixed required counts per section means independent combination choices: C(5,4) * C(6,3) = 5 * 20 = 100.
explanation_sections.approach: Classify: unordered selection with fixed counts per group. Step 1 - choose 4 from 5 in Section A: C(5,4) = 5. Step 2 - choose 3 from 6 in Section B: C(6,3) = (6*5*4)/(3*2*1) = 20. Step 3 - multiply independent stages: 5 * 20 = 100.
explanation_sections.lesson: When a problem fixes the exact number to choose from each group separately, form the product of the individual C values - this is the fundamental multiplication principle.
explanation_sections.timing: 55 seconds. C(5,4)=5 is quick; spend time on C(6,3)=20. Trap: option 2 inflates by treating one section as ordered.
